Night cooling in enclosed residential courtyards

  1. Siobhan Whitcombe1
  2. Rosalind Laine1
  1. 1 Port Amsel University, Port Amsel, Northmere
DOI
10.5555/fjfs.2026.x001
Running title
Night cooling in courtyards

Abstract

Enclosed courtyards cool more slowly at night than open streets. We compared twelve courtyards with adjacent streets over forty clear nights and found that courtyards cooled 31% more slowly, with the gap largest in courtyards whose sky view factor was below 0.4.

1 Introduction

Courtyard housing is common in older districts of Northmere's port cities.The 1911 building code required light wells in every block deeper than twenty metres. Courtyards provide shade by day, but their walls obstruct the night sky and may slow radiative cooling. Earlier work on residential streets found that dense, enclosed canopy can retain heat; courtyards are an extreme case of enclosure.

We ask whether courtyards cool more slowly than the streets beside them, and whether the difference depends on how much sky each courtyard can see. The study design is shown in Figure 1 and the main result in Figure 2.

2 Methods

We installed paired surface loggers in twelve courtyards and on the street outside each one. Sky view factor was measured from hemispherical photographs taken at each courtyard sensor.Photographs were processed with the same threshold for every courtyard; see the supplementary protocol. Nights were retained when cloud stayed below three oktas and wind below 3 m s⁻¹.

For each pair and night we computed the ratio of courtyard to street cooling rate and modelled it against sky view factor with a random intercept for courtyard.

3 Results

Courtyards cooled 31% more slowly than adjacent streets (ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.77). The ratio rose with sky view factor: courtyards that could see more than half of the sky cooled almost as fast as the street, as Figure 2 shows.Two courtyards with glazed roofs were excluded before analysis.

The association held after excluding the three smallest courtyards and after using air rather than surface temperature as the outcome.

4 Discussion

Courtyards trade daytime shade for slower night cooling, and the trade depends on enclosure. Retrofit options that open part of the sky, such as lighter roofs over stairwells, may help. Night-time exposure in courtyard flats deserves direct indoor measurement.

Letter · Enhanced rendering experiment

Report the cloud screen

  1. Rosalind Laine

Night-time field studies routinely exclude cloudy or windy nights, but the criteria are often unstated.A survey of 40 recent papers found explicit thresholds in only 17. A threshold of two oktas rather than four can halve the number of qualifying nights in a maritime climate. The courtyard study earlier in this sample reports its criteria in Section 2, beside Figure 1.

Authors should state the cloud and wind thresholds, the data source used to apply them, the time window, and the number of nights excluded.
